sources.headline: Netanyahu says Flydubai attacker had 'Islamist radical indoctrination'
sources.text: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesByOlivia IrelandUpdated 1 hour agoIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".Figure caption, Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again." Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel, unlike the UAE.The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero". India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well". Image source, Embassy of India in IsraelImage caption, The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers. The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

Live Updates: Investigators Seek to Establish Motive in FlyDubai Attack
UAE launches Flydubai hijacking and terrorism investigation
sources.text:
The United Arab Emirates' chief prosecutor's office said on Thursday that it had ordered an investigation into the apparent attempt to hijack and possibly crash a Flydubai flight to Israel a day earlier.
The state news agency WAM said that "the investigation team has launched its work into the incident already" and that the probe would seek to determine "the degree to which [the incident] was linked to any terrorist activity or intent."
The case will also seek to establish whether it was a premeditated and planned incident involving other actors or the work of a lone perpetrator.
Meanwhile, the Saudi Arabian Interior Ministry announced that the Flydubai co-pilot suspected of planning an attack on a flight bound for Israel had been transferred to the United Arab Emirates.
The plane's captain and the co-pilot "after their health improved and the medical team cleared them, left the Kingdom heading to Abu Dhabi on Thursday morning... accompanied by the Emirati security team," the ministry said in a statement,
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz had called the emergency on the flight to Tel Aviv "an attempted jihadist terror attack" that was thwarted.
Passengers described rushing the cockpit to assist the pilot after he was stabbed by his copilot, who then put the plane into a steep dive in an apparent attempt to crash the airliner.
Aside from minor cuts and bruises among those who intervened in the cockpit, the passengers — the vast majority of whom were Israeli — were all unhurt. Israeli passengers returned home late on Wednesday after the near-missImage: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP Photo/picture alliance
Why does the UAE have jurisdiction in the case?
Judicial authorities in the UAE have jurisdiction over the incident. This is because the aircraft is registered in the UAE and flies under its flag, the statement said, adding that UAE law applied to crimes committed on board "even if they occur outside the country's territory."
The plane was over northern Saudi Arabia for the majority of the early-morning security incident, with tracking data suggesting it briefly crossed into Jordan before turning around to make an emergency landing at the nearby Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
FlyDubai passengers recount terror after hijacking attemptTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had also indicated the likelihood of the UAE leading any investigation in an TV interview with Fox News.
Netanyahu claims signs of Islamist indoctrination, questions why Omani pilot was bound for Tel Aviv
Speaking on Fox and Friends early on Thursday, Netanyahu said of the suspect, "We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," saying "that appears to be something we're gathering from his personal information," without providing further specifics.
He also said that the accounts of those on board made it clear he had suicidal intent, saying that even "after he was subdued," the pilot was appealing to the air crew to kill him. Netanyahu said he didn't want to make "final conclusions yet," but said the "indications we have now" appeared to paint a fairly clear picture.
Netanyahu also said Israel was looking into an apparent "loophole" with the "full cooperation of the Emirati government" to establish how the pilot was in the cockpit in the first place.
"He was an Omani national and we have constraints that say you can't have pilots from countries that don't have diplomatic relations with Israel. So obviously, he was able to go through that," Netanyahu said.
The Omani copilot's identity has not been made public as yet and his motive is the subject of ongoing investigations.
Asked about the possibility of Iranian involvement in this specific incident amid the conflict in the Gulf, Netanyahu said "it's too early to say." Israeli leaders spoke to the passengers who intervened in the cockpit, like Yaniv Hayoun speaking here to Prime Minister Benjamin NetanyahuImage: GPO/Handout/REUTERS
Israel's Herzog nominates 4 passengers for presidential medal
Israeli President Isaac Herzog plans to nominate four passengers who helped overpower the attacker for the Presidential Medal for Civil Courage.
Herzog and Netanyahu spoke with the passengers when they arrived at Ben Gurion Airport on a replacement flight late on Wednesday.
Herzog named the passengers as Yaniv Hayoun, Shota Musayev, Zvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan.
"You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disater," Herzog said. "Today, the whole world saw the beautiful and courageous face of Israeli society."
The medal is Israel's highest civilian award for heroism. Herzog confers the medal but typically nominees are formally chosen by a committee.
Musayev, a dentist who administered first aid to the severely wounded Indian pilot, told Herzog everyone on board had acted courageously.
"We supported one another on the plane and also when we arrived in Saudi Arabia, and we took care of each other as we should," he said. Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu hailed Captain Smit Machchhar's 'extraordinary bravery'Image: Israel's Foreign Ministry/AFP
The Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, has also received staunch praise from Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu and from India's Narendra Modi. Passengers described how the pilot fought off his attacker despite his wounds and was able to open the cockpit door to let them in to aid him. He was in a stable condition in a Saudi hospital, India's Embassy in Riyadh said on Wednesday.
"In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others," Modi said online. "His valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy."

Transcript
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories A flydubai plane headed to Tel Aviv yesterday made an emergency landing after one pilot stabbed the other in a possible attempt to crash the plane. Most of the roughly 170 passengers were Israeli. Some passengers entered the cockpit and subdued the attacker after the injured pilot unlocked the door. Another flight crew on board then helped land the plane safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The motive remains unknown.
A plane carrying passengers from an earlier flydubai flight that was diverted to Saudi Arabia arrives at Ben Gurion Airport on Wednesday in Tzafria, Israel. Earlier, their flight from the United Arab Emirates was diverted to Saudi Arabia after a violent altercation in the cockpit. A second plane was sent to Saudi Arabia to retrieve the stranded passengers and return them to Israel.

🎧 NPR's Kat Lonsdorf was at the Tel Aviv airport as passengers returned. She tells Up First the arrivals area was packed with journalists and family members as passengers came through: some crying, some smiling and many looking exhausted. One passenger told Lonsdorf he tried to keep his young son calm during the ordeal. Another, a plumber, said he helped subdue the attacker and pulled up on the plane's controls after remembering something he had seen on TV. The incident comes less than a month before Israel's national election and is likely to become part of the campaign conversation in the weeks ahead.
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says he wants fewer generals and admirals — and a military built around drones, AI and what he calls a "warrior ethos." In a speech at Quantico yesterday, Hegseth said he has already cut the number of senior officers by about 10% and wants to reach 20%. He also announced a new military command focused on drones and other emerging technologies, even as the U.S. remains at war with Iran. 🎧 NPR's Quil Lawrence says the issue is less about shrinking the top ranks than about who Hegseth is removing and why. Hegseth has blocked some colonels from becoming generals without publicly explaining the decisions and has fired several senior officers. Lawrence also notes that the Pentagon has not held a news briefing since May, which is a stark contrast to the previous two decades of sometimes intense warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan. The FBI says it is "aggressively" investigating a cyberattack claimed by ShinyHunters after the group said it stole sensitive FBI employment data. It is still unclear how much information was taken or whether hackers got in through third-party software or the bureau's own systems. Some current and former employees told NPR the stolen files may include job applications, promotion records, family details and medical information.
President Trump is traveling to Oklahoma today — not a battleground state but a place where he can test-drive his midterm message with a friendly crowd. Trump promised to campaign for Republicans in 35 competitive races, but his first stops are in reliably red states like Oklahoma and Alabama. 🎧 NPR's Franco Ordoñez says that the trips are partly about energizing voters who reliably turn out for Trump but may be harder to motivate when he isn't on the ballot. Oklahoma also gives Trump a lower-risk place to try out campaign lines before heading to more competitive states, where his presence could just as easily motivate Democrats and independents. In an aerial view, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve storage at the Bryan Mound site is seen on October 19, 2022 in Freeport, Texas.

The U.S. has drawn heavily from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve since the war with Iran began, shrinking the stockpile by more than 30% in six months. The reserve, stored in underground salt caverns in Louisiana and Texas, is one of the government's main tools for easing pressure on gas prices. Here's what to know: 🛢️ Rapid drawdowns can damage the reserve itself, putting stress on the salt caverns and other infrastructure.🛢️ The Trump administration is exploring a possible oil swap with Venezuela, though much of the crude under discussion is heavy and difficult to extract.🛢️ China has also tapped its reserves, but less aggressively as electric vehicles make up a larger share of transportation there. Tristan Buckmaster is a mathematician at New York University. He poses for a portrait in his office in Manhattan on September 11, 2026. Buckmaster and his collaborator Levent Alpöge have been working on the Navier-Stokes equations. They are clashing with OpenAI, which claims to have cracked the equations.

OpenAI says its AI helped solve one of math's hardest problems. The catch? Mathematicians weren't quite sure how it got there. That's what I discovered when I started talking to mathematicians about what was supposed to be one of the biggest discoveries this century. It turned out OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model was not some machine supergod that outstripped human intellect – it was just that it was really bad at showing its work.

More details emerge about FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash plane

By
Kerry Breen
News Editor
Kerry Breen is a news editor at CBSNews.com. A graduate of New York University's Arthur L. Carter School of Journalism, she previously worked at NBC News' TODAY Digital. She covers current events, breaking news and issues including substance use.

Updated on: October 1, 2026 / 4:08 PM EDT

Add CBS News on Google
One day after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his identity and motive continued to swirl Thursday. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.There were 174 people aboard the plane. No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday. Who was the FlyDubai co-pilot? The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified. An Omani official confirmed to CBS News that the attacker was born in Oman and currently holds Omani citizenship, but the Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
A FlyDubai flight bound for Dubai is seen before taking off from Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv on Sept. 30, 2026.
Jack GUEZ /AFP via Getty Images
Co-pilot's motive unknownThe co-pilot's motive in the alleged attack remains unknown. Netanyahu speculated to CBS News on Wednesday that the incident looked "like a suicide attempt," referring to witnesses who said the co-pilot had tried to jam the plane's equipment instead of stabilizing the aircraft. After passengers subdued the co-pilot, he shouted for someone to kill him, Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday. In the same interview with Fox, Netanyahu said "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning had led Israel to the conclusion that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination." He did not offer more information.
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday called the incident "an attempted jihadist terror attack," and referred to the co-pilot as a "terrorist." President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing." "We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."His comments went further than Netanyahu's, who told Fox it was "too early to say" if Iran was involved.
An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and were also probing whether the attacker was working alone. Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Co-pilot to be questioned in UAE The co-pilot was placed under arrest immediately. He was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities" on Wednesday, Netanyahu said. Netanyahu said Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly," but did not say when that might happen. Netanyahu did not specify whether the questioning that led investigators to believe the co-pilot had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination" was carried out by Saudi or Israeli authorities. A senior Israeli official told CBS News' Dov Lieber on Thursday that United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan personally told Netanyahu on Wednesday that he expected Saudi authorities to transfer the co-pilot to the UAE for questioning.Saudi Arabia said Thursday afternoon that the co-pilot had been transferred to the UAE, the Associated Press reported.
